Saul is defeated and dies (verses 1–7)

We cannot determine anyone's spiritual or eternal state merely from the way that person dies.

Death comes to the righteous and the wicked.

Saul was badly wounded and could neither resist nor flee.

Yet he showed no concern for his immortal soul.

His only stated concern was that the Philistines might insult him or cause him pain.

He then took his own life.

Henry condemns that final action as sinful.

He also warns that the devil tempts people in great distress to believe such a desperate act is an answer to suffering.

We should guard against that temptation by understanding its moral seriousness before God and the grievous consequences it can bring to others.

But our real security does not come from our own strength.

It comes from the Lord who keeps Israel.

Let us watch and pray, and put on the whole armor of God, so that we may stand firm in the evil day and remain standing after the conflict.

The men of Jabesh-gilead retrieve Saul's body (verses 8–13)

Scripture records what became of the bodies of Saul and his sons.

It does not say what became of their souls after death.

Hidden things do not belong to us.

The way we die, or what happens afterward to our physical remains, matters far less than our eternal relation to God.

If our souls are saved, our bodies will be raised incorruptible and glorious.

But refusing to fear the One who can destroy both body and soul in hell is extreme folly.

The honor people give the dead cannot help those suffering under God's judgment.

Impressive funerals, magnificent monuments and generous praise may preserve a person's public reputation.

Yet those things cannot change the soul's condition.

We should therefore seek the honor that comes from God alone.

[1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.7]
Chapter 31
Chapter Outline
Saul's defeat and death. | (1-7) |
Saul's body rescued by the men of Jabesh-gilead.
(8-13)
Verses 1-7
We cannot judge of the spiritual or eternal state of any by the manner of their death; for in that, there is one event to the righteous and to the wicked. Saul, when sorely wounded, and unable to resist or to flee, expressed no concern about his never-dying soul; but only desired that the Philistines might not insult over him, or put him to pain, and he became his own murderer. As it is the grand deceit of the devil, to persuade sinners, under great difficulties, to fly to this last act of desperation, it is well to fortify the mind against it, by a serious consideration of its sinfulness before God, and its miserable consequences in society. But our security is not in ourselves. Let us seek protection from Him who keepeth Israel. Let us watch and pray; and take unto us the whole armour of God, that we may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
[1Sam.31.8-1Sam.31.13]
Verses 8-13
The Scripture makes no mention what became of the souls of Saul and his sons, after they were dead; but of their bodies only: secret things belong not to us. It is of little consequence by what means we die, or what is done with our dead bodies. If our souls are saved, our bodies will be raised incorruptible and glorious; but not to fear His wrath, who is able to destroy both body and soul in hell, is the extreme of folly and wickedness. How useless is the respect of fellow-creatures to those who are suffering the wrath of God! While pompous funerals, grand monuments, and he praises of men, honour the memory of the deceased, the soul may be suffering in the regions of darkness and despair! Let us seek that honour which cometh from God only.
